record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: Can data-sanitization and network-pruning defenses for data poisoning be used in federated settings without privacy loss, or do federated systems require new defenses that do not rely on direct client data access or representative holdout data?

evidence.quote: whether data sanitization methods and network pruning methods can be used

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which a central server coordinates the training of a shared model with a set of client devices. Each client holds a local dataset that is never directly transmitted to the server; only model updates (e.g., gradients or parameter deltas) are shared. A subset of clients may be adversarial and attempt a data poisoning attack by injecting maliciously crafted training examples into their local datasets in order to degrade the global model or implant a backdoor.

In the centralized (non-federated) setting, two standard families of defenses against data poisoning are:
(i) Data sanitization defenses, which inspect the training data, identify anomalous or malicious examples, and remove or correct them before training; and
(ii) Network pruning defenses, which inspect activations of the trained model on a representative holdout set of clean data and remove neurons whose behavior is consistent with backdoor or poisoning artifacts.

Both families typically assume direct access either to the raw training data or to a representative clean holdout dataset — assumptions that are incompatible with the federated setting, where client data is private and the server may not possess a representative clean holdout sample.

Question: Determine whether data sanitization defenses and network pruning defenses can be adapted to the federated learning setting without compromising the privacy guarantees that motivate federated learning (i.e., without requiring direct server access to client data or to a representative holdout dataset). Either:
(a) exhibit concrete adaptations of data sanitization and network pruning that retain provable defensive guarantees against data poisoning while operating only on information that does not violate federated privacy constraints; or
(b) establish that no such adaptation is possible and that federated systems must instead rely on fundamentally new poisoning defenses that do not depend on direct client data access or representative clean holdout data.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers (2024–2025) on federated learning security continue to discuss data sanitization and pruning-style defenses as active research directions, with proposed adaptations such as Federated Data Sanitization Defense via federated clustering of model updates. However, these proposals rely on heuristics over update statistics rather than provably privacy-preserving direct sanitization, and no consensus exists that the centralized defenses can be transported to the federated setting without privacy loss. The question remains an open research direction.

status_evidence.title: Anomaly detection and defense techniques in federated learning: a comprehensive review
status_evidence.snippet: Defense mechanisms against security threats include sniper, pruning, data sanitization, FoolsGold, outlier detection, robust aggregation, etc.
status_evidence.claim: Sanitization and pruning are still listed as candidate defenses but their direct federated applicability remains an active research topic.

status_evidence.title: Distributed clustering meets federated learning: a clustering-based approach to data poisoning mitigation
status_evidence.snippet: Federated Data Sanitization Defense leverages federated clustering to group model updates based on semantic consistency, identifying and isolating outlier updates.
status_evidence.claim: Proposed federated adaptations of sanitization operate on model updates rather than raw data, and provable privacy-preserving guarantees are not established.

status_evidence.title: Federated Learning Attacks Revisited: A Critical Discussion of Gaps, Assumptions, and Evaluation Setups
status_evidence.snippet: Critical discussion of gaps, assumptions, and evaluation setups for FL attacks and defenses.
status_evidence.claim: Gaps remain in adapting classical defenses to the federated setting under realistic privacy assumptions.
